passage:
Playschool note, Tuesday
At circle time, Jatin, 5, told us he saw a green monster behind the slide at the park, "with three eyes and a long tail". He wasn't joking; he looked worried.
Later I read our storybook. Its monster has three eyes and a long tail. Jatin pointed. "That's the one I saw!"
He remembers the monster clearly but has mixed up the book with the park.
I told him, "That monster lives in the book. Let's check the park together." We peeped behind the slide and found a green watering can. He laughed.
Amandeep

qa.q: What was really behind the slide?
qa.a: A green watering can was behind the slide.

qa.q: Why did Jatin look worried at circle time?
qa.a: He truly believed he had seen the monster at the park, because he remembered it clearly but had lost track that it came from the storybook.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do to help Jatin, and why is it gentle?
qa.a: Amandeep said the monster lives in the book and checked behind the slide with Jatin, so he could see for himself without being called a liar.

qa.q: How might the other children at circle time feel hearing about the monster?
qa.a: Some might feel scared of the park, so checking it together could help them feel safe too.

grounding: It shows a preschool boy who says he saw a monster at the park when it came from a storybook.

passage:
In the village, Selvam, four, ran home from the play area under the banyan tree. "Amma! A ghost in a white sheet was near the swing!"
Kavitha put down the rice winnow. "Where?"
"Near the swing. It went whooo."
She remembered that their neighbour Ayesha akka had told the children a ghost story the night before, with a white sheet.
Kavitha took his hand and walked to the banyan tree. A white cloth was drying on the fence, flapping in the wind.
"Is this your ghost?" she asked. Selvam stared, then giggled. "Ayesha akka's ghost is in her story."

qa.q: What was flapping on the fence near the banyan tree?
qa.a: A white cloth was drying on the fence, flapping in the wind.

qa.q: Why did Selvam believe the ghost was near the swing?
qa.a: Ayesha akka's story with the white sheet stayed in his head, and he lost track that it came from the story, not the play area.

qa.q: What did Kavitha choose to do instead of dismissing him?
qa.a: She took his hand and walked to the banyan tree with him, so he could see the cloth and sort out the story from what was real.

qa.q: How might Ayesha akka feel if she heard about the ghost?
qa.a: She might smile, or decide to tell gentler stories, since her ghost followed Selvam all the way to the swing.

grounding: It shows a preschool boy who reports seeing a ghost at the play area when it came from a story he heard.

passage:
On Monday in Berlin, five-year-old Adam told his kindergarten teacher, Selin, "I saw a dragon in the park yesterday! It was sleeping under the bridge."
Selin asked, "What did it look like?"
"Blue with gold spots. It snored."
At pickup, Selin told his mother, Nour, who smiled. "On Saturday we read a book about a blue dragon under a bridge. On Sunday we walked past the park bridge."
At home Nour opened the book. Adam pointed. "That's my dragon!" Then: "But I saw it at the park."
"You saw the bridge at the park," Nour said. "The dragon lives in this book."

qa.q: Where did Adam say the dragon was sleeping?
qa.a: Adam said it was sleeping under the bridge in the park.

qa.q: Why does Adam still say, "But I saw it at the park"?
qa.a: He remembers the dragon vividly and really did see the park bridge, so the story and the walk have blended and he has lost track of where the dragon came from.

qa.q: How did Nour help Adam untangle the memory?
qa.a: She showed him the book and calmly said he saw the bridge at the park while the dragon lives in the book.

qa.q: Why was it useful that Selin asked what the dragon looked like instead of saying it wasn't real?
qa.a: Selin's open question let Adam share the details, which later helped Nour link them to the book without making him feel foolish.

grounding: It shows a preschool boy who says he saw a dragon in the park when it came from a picture book.

passage: At the city library's children's corner, Gargi, the librarian, asked what everyone did at the weekend. Chirag, five, shot up his hand. "I saw a monster in the park! A purple one with spiky hair, and it ate the swings!" Neelam, the helper, caught Gargi's eye. On Friday she had read them a picture book about a purple monster who ate a playground. Gargi didn't laugh. "Chirag, where did you meet it: in the park, or in a book?" "In the park." Then his eyes found the purple cover on the shelf. "Ohh. That one." He grinned. "It was in the park in the book."

qa.q: What did Chirag say the monster ate?
qa.a: It ate the swings.

qa.q: Why was Chirag so sure he met the monster in the park?
qa.a: He remembered the monster and the park clearly but had lost track that both came from the picture book, so it felt like something he saw.

qa.q: How did Gargi help Chirag find where the monster came from?
qa.a: Gargi didn't laugh and asked a gentle either-or question, park or book, which gave him space to notice the cover and sort it out himself.

qa.q: Why did Neelam catch Gargi's eye when Chirag spoke?
qa.a: Neelam recognised the monster from the book she read on Friday and wanted Gargi to know the story's real source.

grounding: A preschool boy reports seeing a monster in the park that actually came from a picture book, having lost track of the source.

passage: I'm Harish, Ojas's big brother. On Sunday night Dadi told us about the hairy monster that lives in the old tamarind tree. Ojas, five, listened with the blanket up to his nose. On Tuesday we went to the colony park, and he just played on the slide. But yesterday he told his nursery class, "I saw a hairy monster in the tamarind tree at the park! It waved at me!" His teacher phoned Mummy. I don't think he was fibbing; he told it the way he tells about the slide. He knows the monster well. He just forgot it came from Dadi's story, not the park.

qa.q: Where did Dadi say the hairy monster lives?
qa.a: In the old tamarind tree.

qa.q: Why did Ojas tell the class about the monster so confidently?
qa.a: He knew the monster well from Dadi's story and had lost track of where it came from, so to him it felt like something seen at the park.

qa.q: What could Mummy ask Ojas to help sort out the story?
qa.a: She could gently ask, "Did you see it at the park, or hear about it from Dadi?", letting him find the source without calling it a lie.

qa.q: How might Ojas's teacher have felt hearing about the monster?
qa.a: The teacher was probably puzzled and a little concerned, unsure whether something had really frightened him at the park.

grounding: An older brother notices his preschool brother telling a grandmother's monster story as something he saw at the park.
